blocks.text: The command to “test the spirits” concerns claims made by false prophets, not private intuition alone. The stated test is whether a spirit confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This affirms the importance of Jesus’ embodied coming, but the passage itself does not establish more specific labels for the opponents. The instruction calls for communal discernment and should not be used to manipulate people, silence evidence, or shield religious authority from accountability.

“God is love” is explained here through God’s sending of the Son and through the call to love one another; it is not presented as an abstract slogan detached from truth, embodiment, or material need. Likewise, “perfect love casts out fear” is specifically connected with fear of punishment and confidence for judgment. It should not be turned into shame for people who experience anxiety, trauma, disability, or a need for safety.

The chapter contrasts voices that speak “from the world” with the Father’s sending of the Son into the world as its Savior. The wider letter also cautions against loving “the world” and its desires. These uses should be read in context rather than as a command to hate people, embodied life, culture, or material creation.

Testing spiritual claims means that authority is answerable to discernment. The chapter’s language should not be made to support spiritual abuse, authoritarian leadership, or anti-intellectualism; its repeated emphasis on love also rules out using Christian claims to coerce, shame, or harm others.
The work itself does not name its writer, its addressees, its location, or its destination. Those details therefore cannot be settled from 1 John 4 or the letter’s text alone.
